job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Jade Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a small bookkeeping practice in Paisley, the town next to Glasgow. There are five of us and the boss, Mrs Dunne. I do VAT returns, payroll for about 20 small firms and the odd set of year-end accounts. It's a lot of phone calls with plumbers and hairdressers who've lost a receipt. I rent a room above a chip shop with a flatmate, and my student loan comes out of my pay before I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've heard it before. At work I'd say the computer does a bit of the typing and that's it. I wouldn't post anything online, to be honest, because I don't have a view that others haven't already had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine as long as nothing moves. I'm the youngest and the newest, and the loan takes a big bite, so I've got about two weeks of money in the bank. I don't like surprises, and I'd rather things stayed the way I've learned them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I do now. I'd keep going on my qualification exams on Tuesday nights and not try anything new at work. If the practice started using some software to read receipts, I'd let one of the others test it first and ask them how it went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but a bit tight in the chest when I look at the bank balance. Nothing's wrong, but nothing's comfortable either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do the clients send you their paperwork now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Photos on a phone, mostly. Half the plumbers send a blurry picture of a receipt on WhatsApp and I type it in by hand. There's a program that could read them, I know, but Mrs Dunne says she doesn't trust it with a client's money and I agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the practice got busier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be pleased, because more work means maybe a rise. But I'd also be nervous in case it was a one-off and I'd taken on a flat I couldn't afford. I'd wait three months before I changed anything, and see if the busy lasted.

say: I'd say we've heard it all before and the computer only does a bit of **typing**.
I wouldn't post anything online; I've no view others haven't had.
think: I'd be fine as long as nothing **moves**, but I only have two weeks of money.
I don't like **surprises** and I'd rather keep things the way I've learned them.
do: Carry on exactly as now and keep going to **exam classes** on Tuesday nights.
Let a colleague test any new **receipt software** first and ask how it went.
feel: **Steady**, but a bit tight in the chest when I look at my bank balance.
S0.quote: Nothing's wrong, but nothing's comfortable either.
fieldNote: Her **thin** cushion means even a plateau leaves her anxious, though she sounds calm.
She avoids new tools by habit and trusts her boss's caution about software.
She would wait three months before changing anything, a clear wait-and-see streak.

steps.text: Keep going to exam classes on Tuesday nights
Carry on with the same VAT and payroll routine
Wait three months before changing anything if work gets busier

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of fuss, but I'd keep my head down at work. I'd tell friends that there's still plenty a computer can't do, like talking a plumber through a tax letter. I'm sure I'd say it with more confidence than I'd feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my job is the sort that gets done by software first. It's typing numbers, checking them and filing returns. I think Mrs Dunne would keep us for a while, but she wouldn't take on another junior if one of us left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the practice's training day and learn whatever software Mrs Dunne chose. I'd rather be shown than read about it. I'd save 60 a month, which means giving up the gym, and I'd ask my gran if I could use her spare room for a few months if I lost my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bothered. Like a stone in my shoe that I can't get out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mrs Dunne let the practice change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would, slowly. She's 58 and she's built this on being trusted, so she'd bring in new software only after she'd seen it work at another firm. That suits me. It gives me time, though I don't know how much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your colleagues is most at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcia, who does the payroll with me. She's 51, no qualifications beyond what she's learnt on the job. If a package took over payroll, my colleague Marcia would be the first one the practice couldn't justify. I'd feel awful sitting next to her.

say: I'd say it's a lot of **fuss** and a computer can't talk a plumber through a tax letter.
I'd say it with more **confidence** than I feel.
think: My job is **typing** numbers, checking them and filing, which is what software takes first.
Mrs Dunne would keep us, but wouldn't take on another **junior** if one left.
do: Go to the practice's **training day** and learn whatever software she chooses.
Save **60** a month by giving up the gym.
Ask my **gran** about her spare room if I lost my job.
feel: **Bothered**, like a stone in my shoe that I can't get out.
S1.quote: If a package took over payroll, my colleague Marcia would be the first one the practice couldn't justify.
fieldNote: She is realistic that her **work** is routine, but trusts her boss to move slowly.
Her guilt about Marcia shows she thinks of colleagues first.
Her gran's spare room is the quiet safety net, not money.

steps.text: Attend the practice's training day on the new software
Save 60 a month by dropping the gym
Ask my gran about her spare room as a fallback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not say much at work, if I'm honest, because there'd be no point, and Mrs Dunne would be as lost as me. I'd tell my friends it's gone too fast for anyone to sort. I'd probably say that the people in charge should have thought about this years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have no job within two years and no way of pulling together the money to retrain. Everything I do is the kind of thing AGI is meant to do, and I don't know any other trade. The loan would still be there and I've never been good at being thrown in at the deep end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably sit tight for a month, which isn't clever, but I'd need time to take it in. Then I'd look for any job that needs a person in the room, in a care home or a school office or a hospital's finance team. I'd cut everything to the minimum and tell my flatmate we might have to give up the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd stop sleeping properly, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd phone my gran and my aunt first, probably the same night. I'm not good at crying in front of people. At work I'd put my head down, and I'd go for a walk in the park at lunchtime so I didn't stare at the screen thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your flatmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that same night. Her rent's tied to mine, so it's only fair. We'd probably talk about moving in together somewhere cheaper, and she'd say the sensible thing, which is to start looking now. I wouldn't want to, but she'd be right.

say: I'd not say much at work, because Mrs Dunne would be as **lost** as me.
I'd say the people in charge should have thought about this **years ago**.
think: I'd have no job within two years and no money to **retrain**, and I know no other trade.
The **loan** would still be there, and I'm not good at the deep end.
do: Sit tight for a month, then look for jobs with a **person in the room**.
Cut everything to the **minimum** and tell my flatmate we may lose the flat.
Phone my gran and aunt the **same night**.
S2.quote: Everything I do is the kind of thing AGI is meant to do, and I don't know any other trade.
fieldNote: She expects to lose her **job** and has no trade to fall back on.
She freezes for a month first, then looks for human-presence work.
Support is gran, aunt and flatmate; she dislikes crying in front of people.

steps.text: Look for care home and school office jobs that need a person
Cut spending to the minimum and plan a cheaper flat with my flatmate
Phone my gran and aunt the same night
Wait a month before deciding on anything big

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad it's not the faster one, but I'd say it quietly. At work I'd say we've got time to see what the software can really do. I'd also say that someone should be telling the schools to teach this, for the next lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a breather but not a fix. I'd finish my qualification and be a bit more useful, but AGI would still be doing the work I do. I'd have maybe 5000 saved if I scrimped, and I'd be 27 and having to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the exams in the next two years and save 100 a month. I'd look at the public sector, like the council's finance team or the health service, because those places change slowly and need people to sign things. I'd also finally try the practice's software, so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit better than the fast one. Like waiting at a bus stop in drizzle rather than in a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different about five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be able to take it step by step. I'd go to the council jobs fair and see what they want. I think I'd probably still be anxious but I'd have something to do with it. Having a list helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mend my credit by paying the card down. I'd stop the occasional takeaway and the odd night out. I'd also ask for more responsibility at the practice, like running a few clients on my own, so there's something to put on a form.

say: I'd say I'm glad it's not the faster one, but I'd say it **quietly**.
I'd say someone should tell the **schools** to teach this.
think: Five years gives me a **breather** but not a fix.
I'd be 27 with maybe 5000 saved, having to **start over**.
do: Finish the **exams** within two years and save 100 a month.
Look at **council** and health service finance jobs that need people to sign things.
Finally try the practice's **software** so I'm not caught out.
feel: Better than the fast one, like waiting at a **bus stop** in drizzle, not a storm.
S3.quote: I'd be 27 and having to start over.
fieldNote: She uses the **extra** time for a sensible plan: exams, savings, council jobs.
The trust she places in slow-moving public bodies is typical of her centrist caution.
Trying the software is a big step for someone who has avoided it.

steps.text: Finish the accountancy exams within two years
Save 100 a month and pay down the credit card
Apply to council finance teams at the jobs fair
Try the practice's new software at last

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so nobody should panic. At work I'd say let's see what happens to the software, and I'd go along with whatever the practice does. I'd say that the government should be sorting out a plan, and I'd leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a lot calmer in that one. I'd be 32 and might have cleared the loan and be earning a decent wage. But I do worry I'd put off learning anything until it was too late, because that's how I am. I'd have to push myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the exams, then try for a senior role at the practice or move to a bigger firm. I'd pay the loan off faster, about 200 a month, and start a small pension. I'd also learn one new piece of software a year, so I'm not left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reasonably calm. I'd still keep an eye on it, but I'd be able to sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you stay in bookkeeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the practice kept going, I'd stay, but if it was bought up, I'd go into the public sector. I'd probably retrain at some point, perhaps into something with people in it, like an advice service or an adviser at a housing office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think about your own future in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I see myself in a small house with a garden, working part-time in an advice centre. It's modest, but it's a person talking to a person. If somebody told me in 2026 that this was how it would turn out, I'd say yes straight away.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time, so **nobody** should panic.
I'd go along with what the practice does and say the government needs a **plan**.
think: I'd be 32 and might have **cleared** the loan, but I'd put off learning until too late.
I'd have to **push** myself, because that's how I am.
do: Finish the exams and aim for a **senior role** or a bigger firm.
Pay **200** a month on the loan and start a small pension.
Learn one new piece of **software** a year.
feel: Reasonably **calm**; I'd be able to sleep.
S4.quote: I see myself in a small house with a garden, working part-time in an advice centre.
fieldNote: Ten years eases her **fear** and brings out a gentle picture of her future.
She names her own habit of putting off change, and plans a yearly software step.
Her ideal future is a job where a person talks to a person.

steps.text: Finish the exams and apply for a senior role
Pay 200 a month on the loan and start a small pension
Learn one new piece of software each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. I don't know another trade, I've no savings to speak of and everything I do is typing and checking. What would help is some money while you retrain, a course that leads to a real job, and a boss who tells us early what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think we've all got a plan. I've not. I just do the next thing. It would help if somebody who isn't selling anything told people like me what the next thing should be.

headlineQuote: People think we've all got a plan. I've not. I just do the next thing.
portrait: Jade is a **22-year-old** bookkeeper in Paisley with a student loan, a rented room and two weeks of savings.
She's centrist and cautious, never uses AI tools, and trusts her boss's slow approach to new software.
She doesn't blame anyone: she thinks things move too fast and wishes someone would plan.
She is anxious even when nothing changes, alarmed in the two-year world and only uneasy with ten years to prepare.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because she knows no other trade and has almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** retraining that leads to a real job, and a boss who tells the team early what's coming.
